title: Russian bombing kills 26 people at humanitarian aid centre in Ukraine, Kyiv says
description: Figure caption, Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast craterByJaroslav LukivUpdated 2 minutes agoAt least 26 people were killed after Russi
body: Figure caption, Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast craterByJaroslav LukivUpdated 2 minutes agoAt least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering. He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.The Russian military has not publicly commented.Image source, DSNS / ZaporizhzhiaImage caption, There are fears that the death toll will rise further as a number of people are still under the rubbleZelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed. In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday."This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible"."With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.Image source, National police of UkraineImage caption, The Russian strikes left a huge crater where Ukrainian officials say people were shelteringMeanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble". He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in the next few days after negotiations were suspended in February, with Moscow stepping up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.However, no major breakthrough is expected at the talks that are likely to be held in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates.

schema.headline: Russian bombing kills 26 people at humanitarian aid centre in Ukraine, Kyiv says

title: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise
description: Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of vote
body: Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.Organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, the protest drew many of the alliance's most prominent leaders in a show of strength against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.Protesters waved flags and chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power".It was the latest in a series of protests over electoral roll revision that the opposition says has removed eligible voters to benefit the Bharatiya Janata Party. The BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations.The crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling ground in central Delhi known for hosting major political and cultural events. Some protesters sang and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs, while others waited beneath a large canopy in the colours of the Indian flag to hear opposition leaders speak.Gandhi and several senior opposition leaders arrived at the venue in an open jeep, travelling through crowds of cheering supporters.The event was also attended by Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, alongside leaders of regional parties such as Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav, Mehbooba Mufti, Supriya Sule and Tejashwi Yadav.Addressing the crowds, Rahul Gandhi said those gathered had sent a message to Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar."This is not the voice of a single political party or of politicians. It is the voice of India's youth, women, farmers and workers," he said."We will not allow democracy to be destroyed in India. We will not allow the constitution to be destroyed."Other opposition leaders echoed Gandhi's criticism of the Election Commission. Congress president Kharge said the alliance would continue its campaign until Kumar resigned, while Banerjee pledged to keep fighting against what she described as threats to democracy.Speaking to reporters in Delhi on Sunday, senior BJP leader and federal minister JP Nadda accused the opposition of trying to create unrest and destabilise the government under the guise of defending democracy.He described the rally as a "calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy - in the name of democracy".At the centre of the dispute is an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which has resulted in more than 130 million names being removed from India's draft electoral rolls.The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate registrations and the names of people who have died, moved away or are otherwise ineligible to vote. It says eligible voters who have been wrongly excluded can seek to have their names restored.But opposition parties allege that the process is removing legitimate voters and could benefit the governing BJP in future elections.The controversy deepened in September when The Indian Express newspaper reported, external that Kumar had made key decisions about the revision despite repeated objections from the two other election commissioners.The poll panel said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.Sunday's rally followed weeks of protests over the voter-list revision, including demonstrations by student groups and the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). Last month, Gandhi led tens of thousands on a march from central Delhi's Connaught Place to the Supreme Court, demanding Kumar's resignation.The CJP also backed Sunday's rally but chose not to participate. Its founder Abhijeet Dipke said the group wanted to maintain its independence from established political parties.The event took place under strict conditions imposed by Delhi Police. According to local media reports, organisers were required to end the gathering by 5pm, install CCTV cameras at the venue and ensure that protesters did not march beyond the designated grounds.The restrictions came against a backdrop of tensions over the policing of demonstrations in the capital. On 10 October, several leaders of the CJP were detained during protests against Kumar, while BBC reporters witnessed police dragging demonstrators away and beating some with batons.At Ramlila Maidan, however, the atmosphere was largely peaceful, with people of different ages and professions turning out to express their concerns about the integrity of India's elections."We don't even know if this is a people's mandate or a stolen mandate," Isha, a development sector professional from Delhi, told the BBC.Deepro Guha, a lawyer from Delhi, said he was concerned about the way the revision had been carried out."It's important because voting is the basis of democracy. If people's names are removed without any explanation, there is a problem," he said.

schema.headline: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise

title: Donovan Marx farm attack: Five arrested after South African farmer shot and tortured
description: Warning: This article contains graphic details that some people may find distressingSouth African police have arrested five people in connection with
body: Warning: This article contains graphic details that some people may find distressingSouth African police have arrested five people in connection with a brutal attack on a cattle farmer, who was assaulted and tortured in what has been described as a "senseless and barbaric" act.Donovan Marx, 50, was attacked during a house robbery on his farm in Ventersdorp, a small town in South Africa's North West province, last Wednesday.Marx was ambushed as he returned home, shot and stabbed and had his ears cut off in the horrific ordeal, police said.All five of his alleged attackers were arrested over the weekend, a move welcomed by Marx's wife and family.They added that the "legal process must [now] take its course".The horrific attack has caused widespread outrage in a country which is used to high levels of violence.Police last week explained how the attack on Mark happened.A group of masked men armed with guns approached a worker at Mark's house as he was mowing the lawn, they said in a statement.The attackers then demanded to know where Marx was before tying the worker's hands and feet with cable ties.When Marx returned home, police said two of the suspects allegedly approached him and shot him in the upper body."They [then] dragged him inside the house, tied his hands and feet with cable ties, and allegedly stabbed him."The suspects then ransacked the house and took three firearms from a safe before escaping with Marx's van.The ordeal ended after the farm worker managed to free himself and call for assistance. Marx was rushed to hospital, where he remains, but may need prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his own, local news site IOL reported.South Africa's Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack on Marx, adding there was no "place in our country for such senseless and barbaric acts".The chair of parliament's police committee, Ian Cameron, praised police for the swift arrests and called for a "strong, properly investigated case" to follow.The five suspects, aged between 26 and 56, will appear in local courts on Tuesday and face house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition charges.Some right-wing groups have used such attacks on white farmers, who are often from the Afrikaner community, to say there is a genocide against white people in the country - a claim that has been widely discredited.Although the claims have been dismissed by every political party in the country, including those representing Afrikaners, US President Donald Trump has repeated them and has offered white Afrikaners asylum in the US.South Africa's latest crime statistics, covering the period between April and June 2026, do not specify how many attacks took place on farms and only recorded one robbery in a rural area.However, police data show most victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black.

schema.headline: Donovan Marx farm attack: Five arrested after South African farmer shot and tortured

title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades of fighting al-Shabab
description: Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.Uganda's acting army spokesperson
body: Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time. He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal.Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.Last week, Kainerugaba said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces."As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.On Monday, Magezi said this would mark the end of Uganda's operations in the Horn of Africa country, with Somalia expected to "assume full responsibility for security". The withdrawal comes after Somalia President Sheikh Mohamud met his Ugandan counterpart Yoweri Museveni in Kampala last week.The meeting was planned to discuss Somalia's security situation, as well as trade and economic ties between the two countries. The Somali president reportedly sought to persuade Uganda to extend its military presence. In remarks during the visit, Museveni urged Somali leaders and citizens to unite in the fight against the militant insurgency led by al-Shabab, which is part of al-Qaeda.An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside  about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements. Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency for more than two decades.After Ugandan forces were first deployed to the country in 2007, they played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns. They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.Ugandan troops were involved in successive Africa Union missions, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.This was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support. A 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

schema.headline: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades of fighting al-Shabab

title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
description: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.The remaining
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so."Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases.The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.Speaking to reporters on Saturday night, US President Donald Trump said, external the US is still unsure who the culprits are."We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said.Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they meanThe hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach". Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners. The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

schema.headline: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack

title: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
description: Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian dr
body: Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note – a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts."The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us.""But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.  Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings."My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up.""Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app. Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches."This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident."All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said."It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

schema.headline: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine

title: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court
description: Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.In a ma
body: Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer. "We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said."They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats." "We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November. Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.

schema.headline: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court

title: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash
description: An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.D
body: An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people. The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and  was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself."Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB". Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death."Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said."Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit. "Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post, external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.More than 540 people were on board both trains.

schema.headline: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash

title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
description: Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and
body: Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely."The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce. The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit. A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network"."ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores. The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.Additional reporting by Shiona McCallumHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Click here or use the form below.

schema.headline: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack

title: The US Senate races to watch in this year's midterm elections
description: A Paralympian vs a former TV news anchor - and other US Senate races to watchImage caption, Opponents in Iowa - Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ash
body: A Paralympian vs a former TV news anchor - and other US Senate races to watchImage caption, Opponents in Iowa - Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ashley HinsonMillions of Americans are about to decide the future of the Republican-controlled Congress in a midterm election that will have a significant impact on President Donald Trump's final two years in office.All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber. A four-seat gain by Democrats would give them control - and with it the power to limit Trump's ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration. Billions of dollars are being poured into the 35 races across the country, but only a handful could go either way.There are seven Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report, external.Here, we profile the personalities making waves in these much-watched contests.In a nutshell: This race has been marred by controversy over the appearance of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. The Republican senator of that name faces stiff competition from Mary Peltola and accuses her of introducing his namesake to confuse voters, which she denies.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dan Sullivan is aiming for his third term against Alaska Native Mary PeltolaStory of the race: The race may ultimately be the tipping point state that decides which party controls the chamber if, as expected, Alaska is one of the slower states to reach an outcome. Peltola, a former House member and the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress, has run on a platform of "fish, family, freedom" and has attacked Sullivan's record as Alaska's natural resources commissioner. Two-term senator Sullivan, a long-time Marine Corps reservist who also served as Alaska's attorney general, has accused Peltola's campaign of links to an effort to confuse Republican voters which led to a second man named Dan Sullivan entering the race. The Peltola campaign denies any such link, though the issue is the subject of a state investigation and a justice department lawsuit, which on Sunday was rejected by a judge. Alaska's ranked-choice system also adds uncertainty to the mix, and the state has historically been difficult to poll, with surveys historically underestimating Republican voters.How they got here: Sullivan, 61, only retired from the US Marines as recently as 2024, after a 30-year career that included deployments in to Afghanistan and the Middle East. Peltola, 53, grew up fishing salmon with her father, later becoming the first person born in the state to actually represent it in Congress.In a nutshell: One of the few Republican senators who voted to convict Trump when he was impeached in 2021, Susan Collins has consistently outperformed her party in this Democratic-leaning state, partly by presenting herself as a rebel. Her opponent Troy Jackson, who draws on his background as a lumberjack to persuade blue-collar Mainers he can relate to them, hopes that time is finally running out for one of the  survivors of US politics.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Susan Collins, the incumbent, takes on logger Troy Jackson in MaineStory of the race: Collins is hoping her reputation as a centrist will persuade independent-minded voters in a state that reliably votes Democratic in presidential elections. Now her campaign will test whether Republicans can win by distancing themselves from Trump. Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, entered the midterm cycle as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election. But she has been helped by controversy on the other side of the aisle involving Graham Platner, who was ultimately replaced as the Democratic nominee by Jackson, a former president of the Maine state senate. Both Jackson and Collins oppose Trump's tariffs on Canada, mindful of the impact they are having on this border state. Unlike Collins, though, he favours the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE).How they got here: Collins, 73, began her political career fresh from college in the 1970s and she entered the US Senate in 1997. Jackson, 58, is a logger who became politically active when he helped to lead a protest to block lower-paid workers from Canada entering Maine.In a nutshell:James Talarico aims to end a decades-long electoral drought for the Democrats in Texas - and show that one of the Republicans' main strongholds could be in play for the 2028 presidential election. His match-up with Ken Paxton has become the most expensive Senate race ever.Image caption, Trump ally Ken Paxton (L) faces a challenge from former teacher James Talarico (R) in the Texas contestStory of the race: Republican Paxton knows his party has been winning statewide races in Texas for more than 30 years.Texas State Representative James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminary student, is the latest Democrat hoping to break his party's long losing streak.Texas Republicans are facing a daunting combination of headwinds. It is a challenging national political environment for conservatives and there are several state issues like data centre construction and aggressive immigration enforcement that have cut against their party. Added to that is a controversial candidate, Paxton.The campaign has been acrimonious, with Talarico targeting Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled state House of Representatives for alleged corruption, bribery and abuse of power. Paxton denied the charges and was later acquitted by the state Senate, calling the impeachment a "politically motivated sham from the beginning".Supported by more than $170m in funds from tech mogul Elon Musk, Paxton has attempted to paint Talarico as a liberal who is out of touch with Texans on issues like transgender rights, law enforcement, immigration and energy policy.A Democratic victory here might indicate America's second-biggest electoral prize in a presidential election could be within their reach in 2028 - a notion that could dramatically reshape the nation's political landscape.How they got here: Before he entered public service, Paxton spent 14 years launching and building his own law firm. He served in the state House and Senate before becoming the chief legal officer in Texas.Talarico taught at a middle school in San Antonio, in a neighbourhood he has described as one of the poorest in the state. He has studied theology and names Pope Leo as a "spiritual hero".In a nutshell: This is one of the most bitter contests, with left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed aiming to keep this crucial seat in Democratic hands. He is up against Mike Rogers, a Republican former FBI agent who received a surprise endorsement from El-Sayed's defeated Democratic rival, only adding to the acrimony that has characterised this race from the start.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Former public health official El-Sayed (L) will contest Michigan with former congressman Rogers (R)Story of the race: A doctor and public health official, El-Sayed is one of the most left-wing Senate nominees this election cycle. He supports a government-run health insurance system and the abolition of ICE. His strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension in the party.Rogers, who emphasises his military and intelligence background, has managed to maintain Trump's support despite decrying his Canada tariffs and his Russia diesel deal. He has also diverged from the president by calling for a quick end to the war with Iran. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate. As well as attacking him for his politics, Trump and Rogers have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood; El-Sayed has denounced the organisation. The president has also invoked 9/11 and even called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.How they got here: El-Sayed, 41, was born and raised in Michigan before his medical studies in the US and UK and subsequent work in the sector. Rogers, 63, served in the US Army and in the FBI before entering Congress and emerging as a key advocate of US surveillance policies.In a nutshell: Trump made the trip to Iowa on his final day of campaign rallies, such is its importance. Polls have it as a toss-up between Republican and former TV news host Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, who won gold at basketball at two Paralympic Games.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ashley Hinson, who was once a local news reporter, is up against ex-basketballer Josh Turek in IowaStory of the race: Farms, tariffs and Trump have all emerged as key issues in the closely-watched race. Hinson has slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important. Meanwhile, Turek argues that Trump's tariffs have led to "farmageddon" in the largely rural state. He has also sought to convince voters that the war in Iran has led to rising fuel and fertiliser costs. Hinson has cast Turek as a candidate who would vote as an "East Coast liberal". The two have also clashed on issues ranging from taxes and social security to immigration. The last time a Democrat won a federal election in Iowa was nearly 20 years ago.How they got here: Hinson, 43, is a former local news reporter who says her journalistic background helps her understand the issues faced by the state's farmers and small businesses. Turek, 47, was born with spina bifida, going through multiple surgeries before representing the USA at wheelchair basketball at four Paralympic Games, twice triumphantly.In a nutshell: A Democratic victory in Kansas would upend 94 years of history - the last time this Midwestern state elected a Democratic senator was 1932. Senator Roger Marshall is the Republican trying to avoid a humbling defeat, while first-time candidate and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton is the Democrat trying to break records.Image caption, In Kansas, both the incumbent Roger Marshall (L) and the challenger Adam Hamilton (R) highlight that they are fifth-generation KansansStory of the race: Marshall has closely aligned himself as a Trump-aligned, pro-farmer candidate.Hamilton, who once considered running as an independent, has pitched himself as a candidate that can bridge the partisan divide. He has largely campaigned on a message of lower costs and protecting healthcare access. Marshall has sought to attack Hamilton's record as a pastor, describing him as "too woke" for the conservative state. Marshall, meanwhile, has been under scrutiny ever since reports emerged that he sued patients unable to pay their medical bills. He told Fox News the story was a hit job by the left media and senior Democrats. The tight race is broadly seen as a potentially ominous sign for Republicans. A Hamilton victory would be seen as a sign of increasing dissatisfaction with Trump's policies - particularly on economics - in territory that was once considered safe for the party.How they got here: Both Marshall, 66, and Hamilton, 62, highlight that they are fifth-generation Kansans who are in close touch with local issues. Marshall worked for 25 years as an obstetrician, delivering some 5,000 babies, while his rival Hamilton founded a church which became the centre of the largest United Methodist congregation in America.In a nutshell:Trump won this state with ease in 2024 and no-one a year ago considered it in play for the midterms. But Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck and neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown who is running to get his old job back, having represented Ohio in the Senate for many years before losing his seat.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Ohio race sees Jon Husted (L), who replaced JD Vance, compete against Sherrod Brown (R), who is aiming for a comebackStory of the race:Husted was appointed in 2025 to the Senate seat vacated by Vice-President JD Vance, and is now running to serve the rest of Vance's term. He promises to use his business experience to bring jobs and growth to Ohio. In a different election cycle he would probably be the favourite to win this onetime swing state that has become reliably red in the Trump era. But Husted is facing a formidable challenge from Brown, who has high name recognition from three decades representing Ohio in Congress. Brown is known as a champion of workers and was advocating economic populist policies long before others in his party. The race is a referendum on Trump's economic policies, in particular his trade wars that have impacted the manufacturing and auto industries that underpin Ohio's economy.How they got here: Husted, 59, began life in a foster home and was in the world of business before politics; he was an elite American football player at college and his physique has been repeatedly praised by President Trump at rallies. Brown, 73, was introduced to political activism from a young age and was recruited into local politics even before graduating from Yale.By Bernd Debusmann, Daniel Bush and Anthony Zurcher in Washington, and James FitzGerald and Tom Geoghegan in London.What questions do you have about the midterm elections? Click here or use the form below. Get in touchWhat questions do you have?

title: Judge orders Trump administration to stop election official threats
description: A federal judge has ordered the federal government to stop threatening local and state election officials with criminal charges over their role in pro
body: A federal judge has ordered the federal government to stop threatening local and state election officials with criminal charges over their role in processing election ballots. The California judge ruled that the Department of Justice (DoJ) must stop demanding that local and state election officials set aside or not process certain ballots that the Trump administration alleges may come from non-citizens.The ruling comes days before the midterm elections, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency. Trump criticised the ruling on Saturday, writing,"Why would they reject fixing Election Fraud?"In California earlier this month, the justice department sent letters to the secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents. About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security  delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots. Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rareBut the groups said they could not comply with those demands because they must follow election procedures required by state and federal law. A judge weighed in and tossed the demand, writing it would "wreak havoc" in the election.Around the same time, the justice department reportedly began a criminal investigation into county election officials, issuing federal grand jury subpoenas.Civil rights groups and unions representing election workers filed a legal complaint, accusing the justice department of interfering in their duty to administer the election. Judge Trina Thompson ordered the administration to halt their actions."Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters," Judge Thompson wrote.The Trump administration sent a similar letter about alleged non-citizen voters to Washington state and demanded that the secretary of state there cease processing the ballots, according to Thompson's order.The manoeuvres are part of a yearslong campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare. Ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, the president has cast doubt on the security of the vote - alleging "rampant" cheating in postal voting and non-citizens voting. The president also offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud in the US which lead to a conviction.Studies, however, suggest actual cases are extremely rare. BBC Verify reported that the Heritage Foundation's database identified 24 cases of non-citizens being convicted for voting between 2005 and 2025.In his post on Saturday, Trump said criticised recent rulings against his administration pertaining to allegations of possible election fraud and vowed to continue fighting for "Election Integrity".

schema.headline: Judge orders Trump administration to stop election official threats

title: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime
description: Warning: Distressing content and strong languageSamira says she never used to be political."I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BB
body: Warning: Distressing content and strong languageSamira says she never used to be political."I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BBC Panorama.But that all changed the day her only child was shot dead in front of her by Iranian security forces. Sixteen-year-old Sevda was taking part in protests against Iran's repressive regime that engulfed the country earlier this year - before the US and Israel launched widespread air strikes which killed the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.Samira's grief became fury as Iran's authorities then hindered, rather than helped, her search for her daughter's body, she says."I realised that finding Sevda wasn't the end, but just the beginning of all the harassment they put me through."Samira made a dramatic escape from Iran on foot, navigating dangerous mountainous terrain.She now lives abroad in hiding, describing herself as a "one-woman army fighting the regime". In a search for accountability and justice after her daughter's death, she is intent on naming the members of the security forces and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the protests."They'll bring me to the brink of death before they kill me, but finding me won't be easy… Return to normal life? There is no going back," she says.Samira is among several Iranians the BBC has spoken to since the start of the year. Some, still inside the country, told Panorama they wanted to speak out despite the risks, saying they had found it difficult to hold on to hope once the mass protests had been brutally crushed.The Iranian embassy in London told Panorama that peaceful and legitimate protests had been hijacked by foreign powers, including the US, which promoted violence, provided weapons and equipment, and compromised public security.Sevda was killed on 9 January as she and Samira took part in huge demonstrations on the outskirts of the capital Tehran which had begun the previous month. They had been sparked by economic discontent, before escalating into calls for an end to the country's Islamic Republic.Though Samira denies she was especially political then, she says her daughter was. Sevda's idols were two other young women - Mahsa Amini, whose death in custody after an alleged violation against the mandatory headscarf triggered mass protests, and Nika Shakarami, who was killed during a subsequent uprising against Iran's strict Islamic dress code for women."She kept them alive in her thoughts and always wanted to continue their path [of resistance]," Samira says.The day before Sevda was killed, the numbers protesting had been particularly high. Samira says she and Sevda had responded to a call by Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah (king), for demonstrations. "The security forces had lost control," she says.The swell in numbers had spooked Iran's government, and the following day a shoot-to-kill order was announced, Samira says. But she had thought it just an empty threat."They lied so much in Iran… We couldn't imagine a massacre of that scale."And they were reassured, she says, by US President Trump's promise that he had their backs.He had told US media on 8 January: "I have let [the Iranian authorities] know that if they start killing people, which they tend to do during their riots… we're going to hit them very hard."But nevertheless the crowds appeared smaller on the 9th, Samira says. Sevda seemed to know the risks, she says. Her daughter took off her earrings and gave them to her grandmother. She also shared her phone passcode with Samira.The mother and daughter gathered with the rest of the protesters. Sevda then stood on a dustbin and began leading a chant."It seemed there were more forces than people," Samira says of the area where they were. "I don't know how, within one day, they gathered so many… Basijis and IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] forces."The IRGC defends the country's Islamic establishment, and the paramilitary Basij Resistance Force are volunteers for the IRGC."A sniper fired from the roof of a building on our right. The bullet must have come from the rooftop. The bullet went through her heart. I couldn't even scream. I just stared at Sevda - her body lying lifeless. Blood was gushing out her mouth and nose. I couldn't believe it, I couldn't believe she was dying. Her eyes were still looking at me."Samira says she managed to get Sevda to hospital and she was told they were operating on her, but then the door opened and she saw Sevda had been zipped into a body bag.Sevda's body was taken away. Samira says it took her days to find her daughter again. Like many others, she found herself at one of Tehran's largest morgues."Teenagers - young boys and girls. So many had been killed," she cries."I died with every bag I unzipped. I'd never seen so many bodies. But I wouldn't give up."She finally found her daughter. "Three bodies were piled on top of Sevda. That's how we found her."Iranian authorities acknowledge that more than 3,000 people were killed in the protests, but claim some were members of the security forces. One human rights group, Hrana, however, estimates the number of dead stands at more than 7,000, most of them protesters. Finding Sevda's body was just the beginning of Samira's battle with the authorities, she says.To be allowed to take away the body for burial, she says she was forced to say that "terrorists" rather than the security forces had been responsible for Sevda's death."They did this to cover up what they'd done on 8 and 9 January, to hide how many people they had killed. They silenced families by telling them to say their loved ones were killed by Israeli or American terrorists."Nevertheless she was barred from visiting the grave after the funeral, or organising a tombstone, she says.And Samira says the harassment continued. A few days before the ceremony to mark 40 days since Sevda died - highly significant in Iranian culture - she says she was summoned by a local branch of the Ministry of Intelligence."They told me: 'You should give us an interview and say that Sevda was a Basiji and she was killed by the protesters. Then we will announce her [as] a martyr - you will then receive perks, a house, or anything that you want.'"She is sure this offer was prompted by fear, because she had shared Sevda's death with an Iranian media organisation based in London, once the internet had been reconnected in the country."It scared them that I was in touch with external networks or those outside Iran."To avoid giving the interview, Samira fled Iran as soon as the 40th day anniversary was over."I didn't want to trade with my child's blood."She says people smugglers helped her to escape. She crossed rivers and mountains to get to safety.A video she made of herself fleeing makes clear her fury."This crap government, these bastards, they've harassed me so much," she tells the camera as she marches along a mountain path bordered by a deep ravine.Samira says after she continued to give interviews to foreign media from abroad, she was charged in absentia with a string of offences, including "moharebeh" - waging war against God - which can carry the death penalty.To mark what would have been Sevda's 17th birthday, her relatives and friends held a vigil - with Samira watching from exile on a livestream."Then suddenly, the feed cut out," she says.She discovered that the event had been raided, she says, and some of her family and friends arrested by the IRGC.She says her family was warned by the authorities that, if they continued to gather at Sevda's grave, her body would be exhumed and moved elsewhere.Now, Samira shares the names, online, of Iranian security force members and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the 8 and 9 January protests she and Sevda joined."I want justice to be served for every single person whose name I expose, because they have killed so many young people. My goal is for them to be identified so they can be put on trial," she says.When one of the men Samira named online was later found dead, a regime supporter offered a $5,000 (£3,732) reward for information about her whereabouts, presuming she was responsible. Iranian state media has since reported the arrest of nine people in connection with the death.Despite the risks, Samira says she refuses to be silenced."Every day and every second without Sevda is very difficult for me. It's like a mother who has lost her heart, who has lost her being, has lost her life…"But the fact that Sevda is not breathing has made it possible for me to stand on my feet… to think about honouring her life and her path... all those bodies I saw, all those body bags I opened looking for Sevda, they all made me fight the Islamic Republic until my last breath."

schema.headline: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime

title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
description: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC MonitoringFighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the f
body: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC MonitoringFighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition."The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping"."It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday. And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday."I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV."I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month. If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

schema.headline: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire

title: Binance hack: Users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto heist
description: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is belie
body: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack.Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back."We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme."The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.

schema.headline: Binance hack: Users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto heist

title: Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old
description: Figure caption, Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crashByNardine SaadUpdated 1 hour agoA 20-year-old copilot was among nine people killed w
body: Figure caption, Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crashByNardine SaadUpdated 1 hour agoA 20-year-old copilot was among nine people killed when a small jet crashed and exploded in Florida on Sunday, according to US media.Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, is reported to have been one of two crew members aboard the Learjet 60 from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it crashed near West Palm Beach.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it would investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have contributed to the crash, and whether human error played a role.One man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the aircraft nosedived on to a street near Cresthaven, nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.Images from the scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street. The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.Figure caption, Officials describe how Learjet flight unfolded before deadly crashThe NTSB confirmed that after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence."We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit was "we're out of time".Figure caption, Three years before crash, young copilot spoke of earning pilot licenceFilgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the fireball.Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."In a 2023 interview with a local news affiliate of CBS News, Filgueiras spoke proudly of receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school."I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes, but I can't drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it's funny."None of the other eight people on board has been identified.The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash.Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.The NTSB said determining the probable cause of the crash will be a "lengthy investigatory process".As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the NTSB.He added that an individual who was in a vehicle near the crash site sustained a leg injury. Image source, Nathalia Filgueiras / ThreadsUnverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash. "When you see that video, it's a jarring thing," Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters at a news conference on Sunday. "It's like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere."Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the crash as a "horrific tragedy".The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants. Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The jet crashed on a six-lane road

schema.headline: Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old
